verdict: Avoid new footwear exposure in Narela-Bawana for now; lend only to Relaxo/Bata-linked component suppliers with clean GST and tight monthly stock reporting.
title: Narela-Bawana footwear: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Narela-Bawana footwear is a cluster of small assembly and component units feeding national brands and wholesale channels, not a branded retail play.** Units buy soles, uppers, adhesives and packaging, assemble, and sell to distributors or job-work for larger players; cash comes in after the distributor sells through, so the unit funds finished stock and receivables. **The sector has low entry barriers because manufacturing is not capital-intensive [7], so pricing power sits with the buyer, not the unit.** Capex is modest (stitching, moulding, finishing) but retail-linked players carry showroom rent — one rated peer runs 116 showrooms, 112 of them rented [5]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether the borrower owns its premises or rents; heavy rent with thin margins is the first thing to price for.**

## What has changed now
**The national demand signal is mixed: Relaxo's FY26 revenue fell 3.1% to Rs 2,702 crore even as Q4 FY26 revenue grew 8.1% to Rs 751 crore with 16.5% EBITDA margin [2][4].** The Q4 recovery followed a GST cut from 12% to 5% that caused downstocking, now largely liquidated, and distributor count rose from 550 to 630 [1]. **Bata's Q1FY27 net profit rose 23% to Rs 64 crore [3], so branded retail is recovering — but that is peer news, not Narela-Bawana news.** Local data is weak: Delhi GST collections grew 2.7% Apr-to-date against India's 6.1%, and Delhi electricity demand grew 6.5% against India's 9.5% [D]. **India-wide exports are down 3.0% Apr-to-date in USD [D], and the repo is 5.5% with a tightening stance [D], so working-capital cost is rising into a soft local demand patch.**

## Where to grow, and where not to
**Pursue tier-2 component and job-work suppliers to Relaxo, Bata and rated exporters — they inherit a recovering order book without carrying brand inventory risk.** A rated peer with 99.9% parent ownership shows how much a strong parent matters to liquidity [6]; prefer borrowers with a named anchor buyer. **Avoid pure wholesale units selling into Delhi's own retail chain and any unit whose sales are mostly cash-to-distributor with no GST trail.** The unorganised sector's presence keeps competition stiff and margins thin [7]. **If a proposal is a standalone unit with no anchor buyer and no owned premises, ask for the last six months of GST returns and distributor-wise sales before anything else.**
**If the borrower cannot produce monthly stock statements, decline — the cycle is too short to lend blind.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch distributor count and stock days at the anchor buyer: Relaxo's distributor base moved 550 to 630 in one quarter [1], and a reversal there hits job-work orders within weeks.** Watch Delhi GST growth versus India monthly [D]; a widening gap means local offtake is stalling. **Watch the borrower's receivable days and any shift from cheque to cash sales — that is distress, not efficiency.** Rating reports here are undated [5][6][7][8], so treat them as background, not current. **Sources say little about Narela-Bawana specifically; this call leans on first principles and peer results, and the local data we do have is negative.**
watch: Filing gap or falling turnover vs prior quarter -> freeze fresh disbursal and inspect stock
Distributor count or orders fall -> shift borrower to secured, shorter-tenor limits
Gap widens beyond current 3.4 pp [D] -> pause new cluster exposure
Delhi growth stays below India [D] for two more prints -> reprice risk on all renewals
